label: rk_alpha0
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rk_alpha0}
The case $\alpha=0$ is closely related to a result of Caffarelli \cite{Caffarelli_1993}, stating that a convex subsolution to the equation $\det\mathsf{D}^2u=1$ on a domain in $\mathbb{R}^n$ cannot vanish on an affine subspace of dimension $n/2$ or higher (see also \cite{CaffarelliYuan2022,Mooney_2015,MooneyRakshit2023}). Indeed, the above answer implies this result by the comparison principle, whereas the shorter proof of the result by Mooney \cite{Mooney_2015} can be adapted to give one direction of the answer for $\alpha=0$ (the other, easier direction is provided by a Pogorelov-type barrier; see below). Nevertheless, even in this case, our proof of the former direction is different from Mooney's, thus giving yet another proof of Caffarelli's result.
head: environment
name: Case $\alpha=0$

label: rk_motivation
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rk_motivation}
For a solution $u$ to a Monge-Amp\`ere equation on a convex domain, ``having finite slope'' (at a boundary point) is essentially a local Lipschitz property and follows on many occasions from the vast existing work on boundary/global estimates for Monge-Amp\`ere equations 
(see e.g.\ \cite{Le_2, Le_3, Le_4, Le-Savin, Mohammed, Savin-Zhang}), whereas ``having infinite slope'' is a less studied aspect. Our motivation for studying the latter comes from affine differential geometry, where ``having infinite slope everywhere on $\partial\Omega$'' (equivalent to $\lim_{x\to\partial\Omega}\|\mathsf{D} u(x)\|\to+\infty$) corresponds to the \emph{Euclidean completeness} of the Legendre dual hypersurface in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. For example, \emph{hyperbolic affine spheres} and their generalization, convex hypersurfaces of \emph{constant affine Gauss-Kronecker curvature}, are given respectively by convex functions $w,u\in C(\overline{\Omega})\cap C^\infty(\Omega)$ satisfying 
$$
\det \mathsf{D}^2 w=(-w)^{-n-2}\  \text{ in $\Omega$},\quad	w|_{\partial\Omega}=0,
$$
$$
\det \mathsf{D}^2 u=(-w)^{-n-2}\  \text{ in $\Omega$, with $w$ as above};
$$
the infiniteness of slopes has been established for $w$ in \cite{Cheng-Yau}, for $u$ in \cite{Li-Simon-Chen} under smoothness assumptions, and generalized in \cite{Li-Simon-Zhao,  Nie-Seppi_1, Nie-Seppi_3,Nie-Seppi_2, Wu-Zhao, Xiong-Yang}.
head: environment
name: Motivation

title: Remark
body_md: Although part \ref{item_thmA2} is stated only for the first equation in \eqref{eqn_introequations}, the same conclusion for the second equation follows  because ${\mathrm{dist}}(\,\cdot\,,\partial\Omega)\leq {\mathrm{dist}}(\,\cdot\,,L)$ and $\alpha\leq 2d-2n<0$. In contrast, in part \ref{item_thmA1}, $\alpha$ does not have a definite sign, hence there is no direct implication between the statements for different equations. Also note that the third equation does not suffer from existence issues: it is known to admit a convex solution whenever $\alpha\neq n$, while the case $\alpha=n$ amounts to the Monge-Amp\`ere eigenvalue problem  (see e.g.\ \cite{Gu, Le_2} for an overview). Moreover, the solution is known to be unique for $\alpha<n$, while a recent work \cite{Zhou} shows the same for $\alpha>n$.

name: Other existence results

label: cor_C
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor_C}
Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be a bounded convex domain contained in a convex cone $\Gamma\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ such that the ridge $L$ of $\Gamma$ has dimension $d$ and contains a flat boundary piece $F\subset\partial\Omega$ as a subset with nonempty interior. 
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
	\item There exists a convex function $u\in C(\overline{\Omega})$ satisfying
	$$
	\det \mathsf{D}^2u\asymp {\mathrm{dist}}(\,\cdot\,,L)^\alpha\ \text{ in }\Omega, \quad u|_{\partial\Omega}=0
	$$
	if and only if $\alpha>2d-2n$. Such a function $u$ has finite slope at $F$ if and only if $\alpha>2d-n$.
	\item\label{item_corC2}
	Let $u\in C(\overline{\Omega})$ be a nonzero convex function satisfying
$$
\det \mathsf{D}^2u\asymp (-u)^\alpha\ \text{ in }\Omega, \quad u|_{\partial\Omega}=0
$$
for some $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$. Then $u$ has finite slope at $F$ if and only if $\alpha>2d-n$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: lemma_AlexandrovMP
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma_AlexandrovMP}
For any convex function $u\in C(\overline{\Omega})$ such that $u|_{\partial\Omega}=0$, we have
$$
		|u(x)|^n\leq C_n\,{\mathrm{diam}}(\Omega)^{n-1} {\mathrm{dist}}(x,\partial\Omega)\mathcal{M}u(\Omega),
$$
where the constant $C_n>0$ only depends on the dimension $n$, and ${\mathrm{diam}}(\Omega)$ denotes the diameter of $\Omega$.
head: environment
name: Alexandrov maximum principle

label: lemma_comparison
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma_comparison}
If two convex functions $u,v\in C(\overline{\Omega})$ satisfy
$$
u|_{\partial\Omega}\geq v|_{\partial\Omega},\qquad \det\mathsf{D}^2u\leq \det\mathsf{D}^2v \ \text{ in }\Omega,
$$
then we have $u\geq v$ in $\Omega$.
head: environment
name: Comparison principle

label: lemma_existence
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma_existence}
Let $\mu$ be a Borel measure on $\Omega$ with total mass $\mu(\Omega)<+\infty$ and $\varphi:\partial\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function which can be extended to a continuous convex function on $\overline{\Omega}$ (cf.\ Remark \ref{rk_extension} below). Then there exists a convex function $u\in C(\overline{\Omega})$ such that
$$
\det\mathsf{D}^2u=\mu\ \text{ in }\Omega,\quad u|_{\partial\Omega}=\varphi.
$$
head: environment
name: Existence of solutions

label: lemma_stability
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma_stability}
Let $u_k:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$, $k=1,2,\cdots$ be a sequence of convex functions converging to a convex function $u_\infty:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ uniformly on compact subsets of $\Omega$. Then the Monge-Amp\`ere measure $\mathcal{M}u_k$ converges weakly to $\mathcal{M}u_\infty$.
head: environment
name: Stability of Monge-Amp\`ere measure

label: lemma_uniform
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma_uniform}
Let $u_k:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$, $k=1,2,\cdots$ be a sequence of convex functions pointwise converging to a function $u_\infty:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$. Then $u_\infty$ is convex and the convergence $u_k\to u_\infty$ is uniform on compact subsets of $\Omega$.

In the setting of Proposition \ref{prop_slopes}, $u$ is said to \emph{have finite slope at $x_0$} if the conditions hold; otherwise, it is said to \emph{have infinite slope at $x_0$}.

label: rk_extension
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rk_extension}
As in much of the literature on Monge-Amp\`ere equations, we assume $u\in C(\overline{\Omega})$ in the above discussions for simplicity, but this assumption is not essential. In fact, every convex function $u:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ can be uniquely  extended to a lower semicontinuous convex function $u:\overline{\Omega}\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ by setting its boundary values to be
$$
u|_{\partial\Omega}:\partial\Omega\to (-\infty,+\infty],\qquad u(x_0):=\liminf_{x\in\Omega,\,x\to x_0}u(x).
$$
This extension belongs to $C(\overline{\Omega})$ if and only if $u|_{\partial\Omega}\in C(\partial\Omega)$ (which requires $u|_{\partial\Omega}<+\infty$ in particular); see e.g.~\cite[\S 4]{Nie-Seppi_1}. Most of the discussions above actually only require $u|_{\partial\Omega}<+\infty$, and do not need $u|_{\partial\Omega}$ to be continuous. 
For example, in Lemma \ref{lemma_existence}, we may only assume that $\varphi:\partial\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ is the boundary value of some convex function $\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ in the above sense (although the resulting solution $u$ might not be in $C(\overline{\Omega})$).
This assumption is equivalent to the condition that $\varphi$ is lower semicontinuous and restricts to a convex function on every line segment contained in $\partial\Omega$ (see \cite[Lemma 4.6]{Nie-Seppi_1}).
head: environment
name: $u\in C(\overline{\Omega})$ is inessential

label: lemma_Lecomparison
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma_Lecomparison}
Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be a bounded convex domain and $u,v\in C(\overline{\Omega})$ be convex functions such that 
$$
0\geq u\geq v \ \text{ on } \partial\Omega,\quad\det\mathsf{D}^2u\leq M(-u)^\alpha\ \text{ and }\ \det\mathsf{D}^2v\geq M(-v)^\alpha \ \text{ in }\Omega
$$
for $\alpha<n$ and $M>0$. Moreover, assume $v<0$ in $\Omega$. Then we have $u\geq v$ in $\Omega$.
head: environment
name: Subcritical comparison principle

title: Proof
body_md:
\textbf{Case $\alpha<0$.} The usual comparison principle (Lemma \ref{lemma_comparison}) has a classical generalization to sub- and supersolutions of the equation $\det\mathsf{D}^2u=F(x,u)$ with right-hand side $F(x,u)$  non-decreasing in $u$ (see e.g.\ \cite[Prop.\ 2]{Cheng-Yau}, \cite[Lemma 6.4]{Nie-Seppi_2}), from which the required statement for $\alpha\leq 0$ follows. For completeness, we now give a simplified proof for the case $\alpha<0$, where $(-u)^\alpha$ is strictly increasing in $u$.

Suppose by contradiction that $u<v$ somewhere in $\Omega$. We may pick $\epsilon>0$ such that
$$
E:=\{x\in\overline{\Omega}\mid u(x)< v(x)-\epsilon\}
$$
is nonempty. Since $u|_{\partial\Omega}\geq v|_{\partial\Omega}$, we have $\overline{E}\subset\Omega$ and $u=v-\epsilon$ on $\partial E$. Then, on the one hand, since $u=v-\epsilon$ on $\partial E$ and $u\leq v-\epsilon$ in $E$, the mass of the Monge-Amp\`ere measure of $u$ on $E$ is no less than that of $v-\epsilon$ (see e.g.\ \cite[Lemma 1.4.1]{Gutierrez}):
$$
\mathcal{M}u(E)\geq \mathcal{M}(v-\epsilon)(E)=\mathcal{M}v(E);
$$ 
on the other hand, by the hypothesis on $\det\mathsf{D}^2u$ and $\det \mathsf{D}^2v$, we have
$$
\mathcal{M}u(E)\leq M\int_{E}(-u(x))^\alpha\mathsf{d} x< M\int_E(-v(x))^\alpha\mathsf{d} x\leq \mathcal{M}u(E)
$$
(the ``$<$'' uses the conditions $\alpha<0$, $v<0$ in $\Omega$, and $\overline{E}\subset\Omega$, the last two ensuring that the integrals are finite), a contradiction.

\textbf{Case $\alpha\geq0$.} Let us first give a proof under the extra assumption $v|_{\partial\Omega}<0$. Suppose by contradiction that $u<v$ somewhere in $\Omega$. By assumptions (note that $u$ and $v$ are nonpositive), the ratio $u/v$ is continuous on $\overline{\Omega}$, and we have $u/v\leq 1$ on $\partial\Omega$ and $u/v>1$ somewhere in $\Omega$. Therefore, $u/v$ attains its maximum
$$
\Lambda:=\max_{x\in\overline{\Omega}}\frac{u(x)}{v(x)}>1
$$
at some $x_0\in\Omega$. The function $w:=\Lambda v$ has the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item\label{item_leproof1}
$u\geq w$ in $\Omega$, with equality attained at $x_0$;
\item\label{item_leproof2} 
$u>w$ on $\partial\Omega$;
\item\label{item_leproof3} 
$\det \mathsf{D}^2w\geq M(-w)^\alpha$.
\end{enumerate}
They follow respectively from the definition of $w$, the inequalities $u\geq v$ and $v>w$ on $\partial\Omega$ (the latter uses $v|_{\partial\Omega}<0$), and a calculation similar to \eqref{eqn_scaledownv}.
By property \ref{item_leproof2}, we may pick $\epsilon>0$ such that 
\begin{equation}\label{eqn_leproof1}
u\geq w+\epsilon\ \text{ on }\partial\Omega.
\end{equation}
Since $(-u)^\alpha$ is non-increasing in $u$, it follows from properties \ref{item_leproof1} and \ref{item_leproof3} that
\begin{equation}\label{eqn_leproof2}
\det \mathsf{D}^2u\leq M(-u)^\alpha\leq M(-w)^\alpha\leq \det \mathsf{D}^2w=\det \mathsf{D}^2(w+\epsilon)
\end{equation}
By the usual comparison principle (Lemma \ref{lemma_comparison}), \eqref{eqn_leproof1} and \eqref{eqn_leproof2} imply that $u\geq w+\epsilon$ in $\Omega$, contradicting property \ref{item_leproof1}. This completes the proof when $v|_{\partial\Omega}<0$. 

The general case can be reduced to the $v|_{\partial\Omega}<0$ case by dilating $v$ as follows. Again, suppose by contradiction that $u<v$ somewhere in $\Omega$. By translation, we may assume $0\in\Omega$ and $u(0)<v(0)$. Dilating the domain of $v$ radially by a factor of $\lambda>1$ and restricting the dilated function to $\Omega$, we obtain the function
$$
v_\lambda:\overline{\Omega}\to \mathbb{R},\quad v_\lambda(x):=v(\lambda^{-1}x).
$$
Since $v(0)<0$, we have, by convexity,
\begin{equation}\label{eqn_leproof2.1}
v_\lambda(x)=v\big((1-\lambda^{-1})0+\lambda^{-1}x\big)\leq (1-\lambda^{-1})v(0)+\lambda^{-1}v(x)<\lambda^{-1}v(x)\ \text{ for all } x\in\overline{\Omega}.
\end{equation}
In particular, $v_\lambda|_{\partial\Omega}<0$.
Meanwhile, the condition $\det\mathsf{D}^2v\geq M(-v)^\alpha$ implies 
\begin{equation}\label{eqn_leproof3}
\det \mathsf{D}^2v_\lambda(x)=\lambda^{-2n}(\det \mathsf{D}^2v)(\lambda^{-1}x)\geq \lambda^{-2n}M(-v_\lambda(x))^\alpha\ \text{ for all } x\in\Omega.
\end{equation}
Replacing $v$ by $v_\lambda$, we may repeat the above derivation of contradiction for $v|_{\partial\Omega}<0$ as long as we pick $\lambda>1$ small enough such that properties \ref{item_leproof1}, \ref{item_leproof2} and \ref{item_leproof3} hold. More specifically, by first letting $\lambda$ be smaller than
$$
\frac{u(0)}{v_\lambda(0)}=\frac{u(0)}{v(0)}>1
$$
and noting that $u/v_\lambda<\lambda$ on $\partial\Omega$ by \eqref{eqn_leproof2.1}, we may assume that $u/v_\lambda$ attains its maximum $\Lambda>1$ at some $x_0\in\Omega$ and set $w:=\Lambda v_\lambda$ as before. We then adjust $\lambda$ and check those properties (with $v$ replaced by $v_\lambda$):
\begin{itemize}
\item By \eqref{eqn_leproof2.1} and the definition of $\Lambda$ and $w$, properties \ref{item_leproof1} and \ref{item_leproof2} hold.
       
                                                                           
   
                                                                   
   
\item 
By \eqref{eqn_leproof3}, we have
$$
\det \mathsf{D}^2w= \Lambda^n\det\mathsf{D}^2 v_\lambda\geq \Lambda^n\lambda^{-2n}M(-v_\lambda)^\alpha=M\lambda^{-2n}\Lambda^{n-\alpha}(-w)^\alpha.
$$
Since $\alpha<n$ and $\Lambda>1$, by decreasing $\lambda$ (which increases $\Lambda$) if necessary, we may arrange that $\lambda^{-2n}\Lambda^{n-\alpha}\geq1$, so that property \ref{item_leproof3} holds.
\end{itemize}
Now that the three properties are established, the rest of the argument is the same as that for $v|_{\partial\Omega}<0$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The shape of the convex cone $\Gamma\cong\mathbb{R}^d\times\Gamma_0$, which is determined by the shape of its proper factor $\Gamma_0$, plays no role in our analysis. For example, when requiring $\Omega$ to be contained in $\Gamma$ as in Theorem \ref{thm_B}, by enlarging $\Gamma$ and applying a linear transformation, we may assume that $\Gamma_0$ is a proper convex cone of any familiar form, say $\mathbb{R}^{n-d}_{\geq0}$ or 
$\big\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{n-d}\,\big|\,z_{n-d}\geq |(z_1,\cdots,z_{n-d-1})|\big\}$.
The main purpose of introducing convex cones and ridges in this paper is to give a coordinate-free exposition.

label: rk_domain
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rk_domain}
	The domain of $u_\lambda$ expands as $\lambda$ increases, and eventually contains any compact subset of $\Gamma$. The statement ``$u_\lambda$ converges uniformly on compact subsets of $\Gamma$'' should be understood as ``for any compact set $K\subset\Gamma$, there exists $\lambda_0\geq1$ such that $(u_\lambda)_{\lambda\geq\lambda_0}$ is defined on $K$ and converges uniformly on $K$''.
head: environment
name: Precise meaning of the uniform convergence

label: rk_homogeneity
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rk_homogeneity}
By a ``$1$-homogeneous convex function on $\Gamma$'', we mean a convex function $f:\Gamma\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $f(tx)=tf(x)$ for all $t\geq0$. Given a hyperplane $H\subset\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}$ such that $H\cap\Gamma$ is nonempty and compact, such a function $f$ is determined by its restriction to $H\cap\Gamma$, which can be any convex function $H\cap\Gamma\to\mathbb{R}$. Requiring $f$ to be continuous is the same as requiring $f|_{H\cap \Gamma}$ to be continuous up to the boundary.  A basic fact which plays a crucial role below is that for any $1$-homogeneous convex function $f:\Gamma\to\mathbb{R}$, the Monge-Amp\`ere measure $\mathcal{M}f$ (defined in the interior $\Gamma^\circ$ of $\Gamma$) vanishes. A proof goes as follows. Given a point $x\in\Gamma^\circ$ and a subgradient $a\in\partial f(x)\subset\mathbb{R}^n$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{equation_homogeneousMA}
f(x')\geq f(x)+a\cdot (x'-x)\ \ \text{ for all }x'\in\Gamma.
\end{equation}
By taking $x'=tx$ with $0<t<1$ and $t>1$ respectively, we infer that
\begin{equation}\label{equation_homogeneousMA2}
f(x)=a\cdot x.
\end{equation}
Inserting \eqref{equation_homogeneousMA2} back into \eqref{equation_homogeneousMA}, we get
$$
f(x')\geq a\cdot x'\ \ \text{ for all }x'\in\Gamma,
$$
which means that $a$ is also a subgradient of $f$ at the origin $0$, i.e., $a$ is contained in
$$
\partial f(0)=\big\{b\in\mathbb{R}^n\,\big|\,f(y)\geq b\cdot y \text{ for all }y\in\Gamma\big\}=\bigcap_{y\in\Gamma}\big\{b\in\mathbb{R}^n\,\big|\,f(y)\geq b\cdot y\big\}.
$$
In the last expression, we wrote the convex set $\partial f(0)$ as an intersection of affine half-spaces. By \eqref{equation_homogeneousMA2}, $a$ lies on the boundary of one of these half-spaces, hence also lies on the boundary of $\partial f(0)$. Since the boundary of a convex set in $\mathbb{R}^n$ has zero Lebesgue measure, we conclude that $\mathcal{M}f$ is the zero measure, as required.
head: environment
name: $1$-homogeneous convex functions on a proper convex cone

title: Proof
body_md:
By the convexity of $u$, for any fixed $x\in\Gamma$, the value $u_\lambda(x)$ (well defined when $\lambda$ is large enough) is non-increasing in $\lambda$.
                                             
    
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          
    
	Since $u$ has finite slope at $0$, the pointwise limit $u_\infty:=\lim_{\lambda\to+\infty}u_\lambda$ exists (cf.\ Definition \ref{def_slopes}).	
	Its $1$-homogeneity follows from the definition of $u_\lambda$.
	To show that the convergence is uniform on compact subsets, first note that 
	since $u_\lambda(tx)-u_\infty(tx)$ is a nonnegative convex function of $t\in[0,1]$ and vanishes at $t=0$, it is non-decreasing in $t$, hence
    $$
    0\leq u_{\lambda}(t x)-u_\infty(t x)\leq u_\lambda(x)-u_\infty(x)\ \ \text{ for all }t\in[0,1].
    $$	
  It follows that if the convergence is uniform on $E\subset\Gamma$, so is it on $\{tx\mid t\in[0,1],\, x\in E\}$. Therefore, we only need to show that the convergence is uniform on any compact set $K\subset\Gamma$ not containing $0$. 
   
   
   Next, by considering a hyperplane $H\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ whose intersection with $\Gamma$ is compact and contained in $\Omega$, we may find a larger proper convex cone $\Gamma'\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ which contains $\Gamma\setminus\{0\}$ in its interior and still satisfies $\Gamma'\cap B_\epsilon\setminus\{0\}\subset\Omega$ for some $\epsilon>0$. Then the pointwise convergence $u_\lambda\to u_\infty$ also holds on $\Gamma'$.
   By Lemma \ref{lemma_uniform}, $u_\infty$ is convex (hence continuous) in the interior $\Gamma'^\circ$ of $\Gamma'$ and the convergence is uniform on compact subsets of $\Gamma'^\circ$. In particular, it is uniform on the above $K$, as required.
head: environment

label: lemma_twodistances
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma_twodistances}
	Given $\Omega$ and $\Gamma$ as in Proposition \ref{prop_d0}, there exist constants $c,\epsilon>0$ such that 
	$$
	c|x|\leq {\mathrm{dist}}(x,\partial\Omega)\leq |x|\quad \text{ for all } x\in \Gamma\cap B_\epsilon\setminus\{0\}\subset\Omega.
	$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $0\in\partial\Omega$ and $|x|={\mathrm{dist}}(0,x)$, the second ``$\leq$'' follows immediately from the definition of ${\mathrm{dist}}(x,\partial\Omega)$. We proceed to show the first ``$\leq$''. As in the proof of Proposition \ref{prop_d0}, we may slightly enlarge the cone $\Gamma$ to obtain a proper convex cone $\Gamma'\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ whose interior contains $\Gamma\setminus\{0\}$, such that $\Gamma'\cap B_\epsilon\setminus\{0\}\subset\Omega$ for some $\epsilon$. 
	After taking a smaller $\epsilon$ if necessary, it holds that 
	$$
	{\mathrm{dist}}(x,\partial\Gamma')\leq{\mathrm{dist}}(x,\partial\Omega)\ \ \text{ for all }x\in\Gamma'\cap B_\epsilon\setminus\{0\}\subset\Omega.
	$$
	In view of the next lemma, we obtain the required inequality.
head: environment

label: lemma_twocones
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: ${\mathrm{dist}}(x,\partial\Gamma')$ and $|x|$ are both $1$-homogeneous continuous functions of $x\in\Gamma'$, so the ratio ${\mathrm{dist}}(x,\partial\Gamma')/|x|$ is continuous in $x\in\Gamma'\setminus\{0\}$ and invariant under scaling. Consider an affine hyperplane $H\subset\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}$ such that $H\cap\Gamma$ is nonempty and compact. The ratio is positive for $x\in H\cap \Gamma$, hence has a positive lower bound $c$ on $H\cap\Gamma$. That is, the required inequality holds for $x\in H\cap\Gamma$. Since any point of $\Gamma\setminus\{0\}$ is a positive multiple of a point in $H\cap \Gamma$, it holds for all $x\in\Gamma$.

name: Shortcuts from the sign of $\alpha$

label: prop_generald
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop_generald}
	Let $\Omega$ be a bounded convex domain in $\mathbb{R}^n=\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^{n-d}$, $u\in C(\overline{\Omega})$ be a convex function, and $\Gamma_0$ be a proper convex cone in $\mathbb{R}^{n-d}$. Assume that 
	\begin{itemize}
		\item The boundary $\partial\Omega$ contains $U\times\{0\}\subset\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^{n-d}$ for a convex domain $U$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ containing the origin.
		\item There exists $\epsilon>0$ such that
		$$
		U\times \big(\Gamma_0\cap B_\epsilon^{n-d}\setminus\{0\}\big)\subset \Omega.
		$$
		\item
		$u=0$ on $U\times\{0\}$.
		\item
		$u$ has finite slope at $(0,0)$.
	\end{itemize}
Consider the family $(u_\lambda)_{\lambda\geq1}$ of convex functions defined by
\begin{equation}\label{eqn_ulambda2}
u_\lambda:U\times\big(\Gamma_0\cap B^{n-d}_{\lambda\epsilon}\big)\to\mathbb{R},\quad u_\lambda(y,z):=\lambda u(y,\lambda^{-1}z).
\end{equation}
Then there exists a $1$-homogeneous continuous convex function $h$ on $\Gamma_0$ such that 
$u_\lambda$ converges to the function
$$
u_\infty: U\times \Gamma_0\to\mathbb{R},\quad u_\infty(y,z)=h(z)
$$ uniformly on compact subsets of $U\times\Gamma_0$ as $\lambda\to+\infty$.
head: environment
name: Directional derivatives transverse to a flat boundary piece

title: Proof
body_md:
The arguments in the proof of Proposition \ref{prop_d0} can be generalized to show that $u_\lambda\to u_\infty$ uniformly on compact subsets of $U\times \Gamma_0$, where $u_\infty(y,z)$ is a continuous convex function of $(y,z)\in U\times\Gamma_0$ which is $1$-homogeneous in $z$. We omit the details. The proof is completed by noting that any such function is independent of $y$, namely $u_\infty(y_1,z)=u_\infty(y_2,z)$ for all $y_1,y_2\in U$ and $z\in\Gamma_0$. To verify this, we use the convexity along the line segment joining $(y_1,0)$ and $(y_2,z)$ to get
	$$
	u_\infty((1-t)y_1+ty_2,tz)\leq (1-t)u_\infty(y_1,0)+t\hspace{1pt}u_\infty(y_2,z)
	$$
	for $t\in(0,1)$. Since $u_\infty(y,z)$ is $1$-homogeneous in $z$ (in particular, $u_\infty(y,0)=0$), by dividing both sides by $t$, it follows that
	$u_\infty((1-t)y_1+ty_2,z)\leq u_\infty(y_2,z)$.
	Taking the limit $t\to0^+$, we get $u_\infty(y_1,z)\leq u_\infty(y_2,z)$. The desired assertion follows by switching $y_1$ and $y_2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
After a change of coordinates, we may assume that $L=\mathbb{R}^d\times\{0\}$ and that the flat boundary piece $F=\partial\Omega\cap L$ contains $U'\times\{0\}$ for a neighborhood $U'$ of the origin in $\mathbb{R}^d$. We claim that there exist a smaller neighborhood $U\subset U'$ of the origin in $\mathbb{R}^d$, a proper convex cone $\Gamma_0$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n-d}$, and $\epsilon>0$, such that 
$$
U\times(\Gamma_0\cap B^{n-d}_\epsilon\setminus\{0\})\subset\Omega.
$$ 
See Figure \ref{fig_infiniteslopeproof}. Indeed, the $d=0$ case of the claim  amounts to the obvious fact that if $0\in\partial\Omega$, then $\Omega$ contains $\Gamma\cap B_\epsilon\setminus\{0\}$ for some proper convex cone $\Gamma\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ and some $\epsilon>0$. For $d>0$, we first apply this fact to the convex domain $\Omega\cap\big(\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-d}\big)$ in $\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-d}$, obtaining a proper convex cone $\Gamma_0\subset\mathbb{R}^{n-d}$ such that the slice $\{0\}\times\big(\Gamma_0\cap B^{n-d}_\epsilon\setminus\{0\}\big)$ is contained in $\Omega$. Then we can use the compactness and the convexity to expand this slice into a region $U\times(\Gamma_0\cap B^{n-d}_\epsilon\setminus\{0\})$ which is still contained in $\Omega$, establishing the claim.

The rest of the proof is a straightforward generalization of the $d=0$ case in \S \ref{subsec_d0}, so we only give an outline. Suppose by contradiction that $u$ has finite slope at $F$. Then Proposition \ref{prop_generald} applies and yields the weak convergence 
$$
	\mathcal{M}u_\lambda  \rightharpoonup \mathcal{M}u_\infty=0\ \ \text{ as }\lambda\to+\infty.
$$
Here, $\mathcal{M}u_\infty$ is the zero measure on $U\times\Gamma_0$ like in the $d=0$ case because when $d>0$, the subgradients of $u_\infty(y,z)=h(z)$ are contained in the null set $\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-d}\subset\mathbb{R}^n$.  Again, we shall reach a contradiction by showing that if any of the conditions
\begin{align}
	&\det\mathsf{D}^2u(y,z)\geq M|z|^\alpha,\label{eqn_generaldproof1}\\
	&\det\mathsf{D}^2u\geq M{\mathrm{dist}}(\,\cdot\,,\partial\Omega)^\alpha,\label{eqn_generaldproof2}\\
	&u<0\ \text{ and }\ \det \mathsf{D}^2u\geq M(-u)^\alpha\label{eqn_generaldproof3}
\end{align}
holds in $U\times\big(\Gamma_0\cap B_\epsilon^{n-d}\setminus\{0\}\big)\subset\Omega$ with $\alpha\leq 2d-n$, then $\det\mathsf{D}^2u_\lambda$ is bounded from below by a positive function not depending on $\lambda$. 

To this end, note that by the definition \eqref{eqn_ulambda2} of $u_\lambda$, we have
$$
\det\mathsf{D}^2u_\lambda(y,z)=\lambda^{-2(n-d)}\lambda^n(\det\mathsf{D}^2u)(y,\lambda^{-1}z)=\lambda^{2d-n}(\det\mathsf{D}^2u)(y,\lambda^{-1}z).
$$
Therefore, condition \eqref{eqn_generaldproof1} implies 
$$
\det\mathsf{D}^2u_\lambda(y,z)=\lambda^{2d-n}(\det\mathsf{D}^2u)(y,\lambda^{-1}z)\geq \lambda^{2d-n}M|\lambda^{-1}z|^{\alpha}=M\lambda^{2d-n-\alpha}|z|^\alpha\geq M|z|^\alpha,
$$
as required. This estimate remains valid under either condition  \eqref{eqn_generaldproof2} or condition \eqref{eqn_generaldproof3}: the former is because, as a generalization of Lemma \ref{lemma_twodistances}, there exist $c,\epsilon>0$ such that
$$
c|z|\leq {\mathrm{dist}}((y,z),\partial\Omega)\leq |z|\ \ \text{ for all } (y,z)\in U\times\big(\Gamma_0\cap B_\epsilon^{n-d}\setminus\{0\}\big)\subset\Omega;
$$
the latter is because, as a generalization of \eqref{eqn_proofpropd02}, there exist $C_1>C_2>0$ such that 
$$
-C_1|z|\leq u(y,z)\leq -C_2|z|\ \ \text{ for all } (y,z)\in U\times\big(\Gamma_0\cap B_\epsilon^{n-d}\setminus\{0\}\big)\subset\Omega.
$$
This completes the proof.

label: lemma_super
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma_super}
	Let $\Gamma_0$ be a proper convex cone in $\mathbb{R}^{n-d}$ and $u$ be a continuous convex function defined on the region
	$$
	D:=B^d_1\times ( \Gamma_0\cap B^{n-d}_1)\subset\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^{n-d}=\mathbb{R}^n,
	$$ 
    which is a neighborhood of the origin in the product cone $\Gamma=\mathbb{R}^d\times\Gamma_0$.  Let $K$ be a compact set in the interior $D^\circ=B^d_1\times(\Gamma_0^\circ\cap B^{n-d}_1)$ of $D$. Then, when $K$ undergoes the transformations
    $$
    \sigma_t:\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^{n-d}\to\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^{n-d},\quad \sigma_t(y,z):=(y,tz),\ \ 0<t<1,
    $$
   its mass with respect to the Monge-Amp\`ere measure $\mathcal{M}u$ of $u$ satisfies
	$$
	\mathcal{M}u(\sigma_t(K))=o(t^{d-n})\ \ \text{ as } t\to0^+.
	$$

label: eqn_subgradientproof0
title: Proof
body_md:
Since enlarging $K$ does not affect the statement, we may assume that $K$ has a product form
$$
K=E\times F,\quad E\subset B_1^d,\ \  F\subset\Gamma_0^\circ\cap B_1^{n-d},
$$
with $E$ and $F$ compact. By compactness, we may pick a sufficiently small $\delta>0$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eqn_subgradientproof0}
\widetilde{E}:=\big\{y\in\mathbb{R}^d\,\big|\,{\mathrm{dist}}(y,E)\leq \delta\}\subset B_{1-\delta}^d,\quad \widetilde{F}:=\big\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{n-d}\,\big|\,{\mathrm{dist}}(z,F)\leq \delta\}\subset\Gamma_0^\circ\cap B_{1-\delta}^{n-d}.
\end{equation}
Note that the last inclusion implies 
\begin{equation}\label{eqn_subgradientproof0.5}
t\widetilde{F}\subset \Gamma_0^\circ\cap B^{n-d}_{t(1-\delta)} \quad \text{ for all }0<t<1.
\end{equation}

Given a point $(y,z)\in \sigma_t(K)=E\times tF$, the subgradients $(a,b)\in\partial u(y,z)$ of $u$ at $(y,z)$ are characterized by the condition
\begin{equation}\label{eqn_subgradientproof1}
	u(y',z')\geq u(y,z)+a\cdot (y'-y)+b\cdot(z'-z)\ \  \text{ for all } (y',z')\in D.
\end{equation}
We proceed to estimate each component of $a=(a_1,\cdots,a_d)$ and $b=(b_1,\cdots,b_{n-d})$. Let
$$
e_1=(1,0,\cdots,0),\cdots, e_d=(0,\cdots,0,1)\in\mathbb{R}^d,\quad f_1=(1,0,\cdots,0),\cdots, f_{n-d}=(0,\cdots,0,1)\in\mathbb{R}^{n-d}
$$
be the standard bases of $\mathbb{R}^d$ and $\mathbb{R}^{n-d}$, respectively. Then 
\begin{itemize}
	\item Taking 
	$(y',z')=(y\pm\delta e_i,z)$ in \eqref{eqn_subgradientproof1}, we obtain
	$$
	\frac{u(y,z)-u(y-\delta e_i,z)}{\delta} \leq a_i\leq \frac{u(y+\delta e_i,z)-u(y,z)}{\delta}.
	$$
	Since $y\in E\subset\widetilde{E}$, $y\pm \delta e_i\in\widetilde{E}$ and $z\in tF\subset t\widetilde{F}$, in view of \eqref{eqn_subgradientproof0} and \eqref{eqn_subgradientproof0.5}, we deduce that
	\begin{equation}\label{eqn_subgradientproof2}
		|a_i|\leq \frac{C}{\delta},\quad i=1,\cdots,d\,,
	\end{equation}
	where $C$ is twice the $L^\infty$-norm of $u$ on $\overline{B}_{1-\delta}^d\times\big(\Gamma_0\cap\overline{B}_{1-\delta}^{n-d}\big)$.
	\item 
	Taking $(y',z')=(y,z\pm t\delta f_j)$ in \eqref{eqn_subgradientproof1},  we obtain
	$$
	\frac{u(y,z)-u(y,z-t\delta f_j)}{t\delta} \leq b_j\leq \frac{u(y,z+t\delta f_j)-u(y,z)}{t\delta}.
	$$
	Since $y\in E\subset\widetilde{E}$, $z\in tF\subset t\widetilde{F}$ and $z\pm t\delta f_j\in t\widetilde{F}$, in view of \eqref{eqn_subgradientproof0} and \eqref{eqn_subgradientproof0.5}, we deduce that
	\begin{equation}\label{eqn_subgradientproof3}
		|b_j|\leq \frac{c(t)}{t\delta},\quad j=1,\cdots,n-d\,,
	\end{equation}
	where
	$$
	c(t):=2\sup_{y\in \overline{B}_{1-\delta}^d,\, z\in\Gamma_0\cap\overline{B}_{t(1-\delta)}^{n-d}} |u(y,z)-u(y,0)|.
	$$
	Note that $c(t)\to 0$ as $t\to 0^+$: otherwise,  there exists a sequence $(y^{(k)},z^{(k)})_{k=1,2,\cdots}$ in $\overline{B}_{1-\delta}^d\times\Gamma_0$ such that $\lim_{k\to\infty}|z^{(k)}|=0$ whereas $|u(y^{(k)},z^{(k)})-u(y^{(k)},0)|$ is larger than a positive constant; then picking a subsequence of $(y^{(k)})$ converging to some $y^{(\infty)}\in\overline{B}_{1-\delta}^d$ leads to a contradiction with the continuity of $u$ at $(y^{(\infty)},0)$.
                                                                            
    
                                                                                 
     
            
    
                                                                                                          
     
                                                                                                                                                                             
\end{itemize}

Since $(y,z)\in\sigma_t(K)$ is arbitrary, estimates \eqref{eqn_subgradientproof2} and \eqref{eqn_subgradientproof3} imply
$$
\partial u\big(\sigma_t(K)\big)\subset \left[-\frac{C}{\delta}, \frac{C}{\delta}\right]^d\times\left[-\frac{c(t)}{t\delta},\frac{c(t)}{t\delta }\right]^{n-d}.
$$
Since $\mathcal{M}u(\sigma_t(K))$ is defined to be the volume of $\partial u\big(\sigma_t(K)\big)$ (see \S \ref{subsec_MA}), the desired conclusion follows.

title: Proof
body_md:
As explained in the first paragraph of the proof of Theorem \ref{thm_A} \ref{item_thmA1} in \S \ref{subsec_generald}, we may assume that $L=\mathbb{R}^d\times\{0\}$, that the flat boundary piece $F=\partial\Omega\cap L$ contains $U\times\{0\}$ for a neighborhood $U$ of the origin in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and that $\Omega$ contains $U\times(\Gamma_0\cap B^{n-d}_\epsilon\setminus\{0\})$ for a proper convex cone $\Gamma_0$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n-d}$ and some $\epsilon>0$.
By further rescaling the coordinates, we may assume that $\overline{\Omega}$ contains $D:=B^d_1\times(\Gamma_0\cap B^{n-d}_1)$.

Suppose by contradiction that $u\in C(\overline{\Omega})$ is convex and satisfies 
\begin{equation}\label{eqn_superproof1}
\det\mathsf{D}^2u(y,z)\geq M{\mathrm{dist}}((y,z),L)^\alpha=M|z|^\alpha\ \ \text{ for all }(y,z)\in\Omega,
\end{equation}
with $\alpha\leq 2d-2n$. Let $K$ be a compact set contained in the interior $D^\circ$ of $D$. Condition \eqref{eqn_superproof1} implies 
$$
\mathcal{M}u(\sigma_t(K))=\int_{\sigma_t(K)}\det\mathsf{D}^2u(y,z)\mathsf{d} y\,\mathsf{d} z\geq M\int_{\sigma_t(K)}|z|^\alpha\mathsf{d} y\,\mathsf{d} z=Mt^{\alpha+n-d}\int_K |z|^\alpha \mathsf{d} y\,\mathsf{d} z,
$$
where $\sigma_t(y,z):=(y,tz)$, $0<t<1$. We may assume that $K$ has nonempty interior, so that the last integral is positive. Since $\alpha+n-d\leq d-n$, 
this inequality contradicts the estimate $\mathcal{M}u(\sigma_t(K))=o(t^{d-n})$ provided by Lemma \ref{lemma_super},  completing the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof is analogous to that of Lemma \ref{lemma_barrier}, so we only present the main calculations. Putting $\gamma:=\frac{\beta}{n-d}$ and $z^{-1}:=(z_1^{-1},\cdots,z_{n-d}^{-1})^{\raisebox{\depth}{$\mskip-1mu\scriptstyle\intercal$}}$, we have
$$
\partial^2_{yy}f=2(z_1\cdots z_{n-d})^\gamma I_d,\qquad \partial^2_{zz}f=\gamma(|y|^2-\Lambda)(z_1\cdots z_{n-d})^\gamma\left[\gamma z^{-1}(z^{-1})^{\raisebox{\depth}{$\mskip-1mu\scriptstyle\intercal$}}-\mathrm{diag}\big(z_1^{-2},\cdots,z_{n-d}^{-2}\big)\right],
$$
$$
\partial^2_{zy}f=2\gamma(z_1\cdots z_{n-d})^\gamma z^{-1}y^{\raisebox{\depth}{$\mskip-1mu\scriptstyle\intercal$}},\qquad
\partial^2_{yz}f=2\gamma(z_1\cdots z_{n-d})^\gamma y(z^{-1})^{\raisebox{\depth}{$\mskip-1mu\scriptstyle\intercal$}},
$$
\begin{align*}
	\partial^2_{zz}f-\partial^2_{zy}f(\partial_{yy}^2f)^{-1}\partial^2_{yz}f=\gamma(z_1\cdots z_{n-d})^\gamma\Big[
	(\Lambda-|y|^2)\mathrm{diag}\big(z_1^{-2},\cdots,z_{n-d}^{-2}\big)
	-\gamma(|y|^2+\Lambda)z^{-1}(z^{-1})^{\raisebox{\depth}{$\mskip-1mu\scriptstyle\intercal$}}
	\Big],
\end{align*}
\begin{align*}
	&\det \mathsf{D}^2 f=\det \partial^2_{yy}f\, \det\left(\partial^2_{zz}f-\partial^2_{zy}f(\partial_{yy}^2f)^{-1}\partial^2_{yz}f\right)\\
	&=\big[2(z_1\cdots z_{n-d})^\gamma\big]^d\big[\gamma(z_1\cdots z_{n-d})^\gamma\big]^{n-d}\det\Big[
	(\Lambda-|y|^2)\mathrm{diag}\big(z_1^{-2},\cdots,z_{n-d}^{-2}\big)
	-\gamma(|y|^2+\Lambda)z^{-1}(z^{-1})^{\raisebox{\depth}{$\mskip-1mu\scriptstyle\intercal$}}
	\Big]\\
	&=2^d\gamma^{n-d}(z_1\cdots z_{n-d})^{\gamma n}(\Lambda-|y|^2)^{n-d-1}(z_1\cdots z_{n-d})^{-2}\big[\Lambda-|y|^2-\gamma(n-d)(|y|^2+\Lambda)\big]\\
	&=2^d\gamma^{n-d}(\Lambda-|y|^2)^{n-d}\left(1-\frac{\Lambda+|y|^2}{\Lambda-|y|^2}\beta\right)(z_1\cdots z_{n-d})^\frac{\alpha}{n-d}.
\end{align*}
Since $\beta<1$, the last expression implies the second inequality in \eqref{eqn_lemmabarrier2}. 
By Lemma \ref{lemma_LA} and the expression of $\partial^2_{zz}f-\partial^2_{zy}f(\partial_{yy}^2f)^{-1}\partial^2_{yz}f$, the first inequality in \eqref{eqn_lemmabarrier2} follows.

title: Proof
body_md:
We begin with the following observation: although the exponent $\alpha>2d-n$ is arbitrary, once the required statement is established for some exponent $\alpha_0$, it follows for all $\alpha\geq \alpha_0$. This is because condition \eqref{eqn_finiteslopeproof1.1} increases in strength as $\alpha$ increases:
	$$
	\det \mathsf{D}^2u\leq M(-u)^\alpha\ \Longrightarrow \ \det \mathsf{D}^2u\leq  M\|u\|_{L^\infty(\overline{\Omega})}^{\alpha-\alpha_0}(-u)^{\alpha_0}\ \text{ for }\alpha\geq \alpha_0
	$$
	(the constant $M$ varies, but this does not affect the statement). Therefore, we only need to treat those $\alpha$ that are arbitrarily close to $2d-n$. Since $2d-n<n$, we may henceforth assume that $\alpha<n$.
	
	Let $f$ and $v$ be the same as in the previous proof, except that we now:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item 
	take the parameter $M$ to be $1$ when applying Lemma \ref{lemma_barrier}, so that we have, in place of \eqref{eqn_finiteslopeproof1.2}, 
	\begin{equation}\label{eqn_finiteslopeproof4}
	\det \mathsf{D}^2f(y,z)\geq |z|^\alpha \ \ \text{ for all }(y,z)\in\Omega~;
	\end{equation}
	the constant $M$ in condition \eqref{eqn_finiteslopeproof1.1} is not used in this step and will appear only later;
		\item 
take the coefficient $C$ to be $C=2C_2/C_1$ in the definition \eqref{eqn_finiteslopeproof0} of $v$;
     \item 
     do not bound $u$ directly by $v$, but will find a constant multiple $\widetilde{v}$ of $v$ to bound $u$ instead. 
	\end{itemize}
By this choice of $C$ and \eqref{eqn_finiteslopeproof0}--\eqref{eqn_finiteslopeproof3}, we have
	$$
     v(y,z)\leq C_2|z|-C_1C|z|=-C_2|z|,\qquad 	v(y,z)\geq -C\xi\cdot z\geq -C|z|,
	$$
	and hence
	$-C^{-1}v(y,z)\leq |z|\leq -C_2^{-1}v(y,z)$
	for all $(y,z)\in\overline{\Omega}$. In view of \eqref{eqn_finiteslopeproof4}, it follows that
$$
	\det \mathsf{D}^2v(y,z)\geq |z|^\alpha\geq C_3(-v(y,z))^\alpha\ \ \text{ for all }(y,z)\in\Omega, \text{ where } C_3:=\min\big\{C^{-\alpha},\, C_2^{-\alpha}\big\}.
$$
Letting $\widetilde{v}=\lambda v$ with a constant $\lambda>0$, we deduce from the above inequality that
$$
\det\mathsf{D}^2\widetilde{v}=\lambda^n\det\mathsf{D}^2v\geq \lambda^nC_3(-v)^\alpha=\lambda^{n-\alpha}C_3(-\widetilde{v})^\alpha\  \text{ in }\Omega.
$$
Since we have assumed $\alpha<n$, we may adjust $\lambda$ to make the right-hand side no less than $M(-\widetilde{v})^\alpha$ (indeed, $\alpha\neq n$ suffices for this purpose). Putting everything together, we have
	$$
	u=0\geq \widetilde{v}\ \text{ on }\partial\Omega,\quad \det\mathsf{D}^2u\leq M(-u)^\alpha \ \text{ and }\ \det \mathsf{D}^2 \widetilde{v}\geq M(-\widetilde{v})^\alpha \ \text{ in }\Omega.
	$$	
Using Le's subcritical comparison principle (Lemma \ref{lemma_Lecomparison}), we deduce that $u\geq\widetilde{v}$ in $\Omega$, and conclude that $u$ has finite slope at $x_0$ as in the previous proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
After a coordinate change, we may assume $\Gamma=\mathbb{R}^d\times\Gamma_0$, where $\Gamma_0\subset\mathbb{R}^{n-d}$ is a proper convex cone such that $\Gamma_0\setminus\{0\}$ is contained in $\mathbb{R}^{n-d}_+$. 
	We apply Lemma \ref{lemma_barrier2} with the same $R$ as here, but with $\alpha$ and $M$ replaced by new parameters $\alpha_0$ and $M_0$ such that
	$$
	2d-2n<\alpha_0<\min\big\{0,2d-n,\alpha\big\},\qquad
	M_0=MR^{\alpha-\alpha_0}.
	$$
	The lemma yields a convex function $f\in C(B^d_R\times\mathbb{R}^{n-d}_{\geq0})\cap C^\infty(B^d_R\times\mathbb{R}^{n-d}_+)$ with
	$$
	\det\mathsf{D}^2f(y,z)\geq M_0\,(z_1\cdots z_{n-d})^\frac{\alpha_0}{n-d}.
	$$
	Since $z_j\leq|z|$ ($j=1,\cdots,n-d$) and $\alpha_0,\alpha_0-\alpha<0$,  we have 
	$$
	M_0\,(z_1\cdots z_{n-d})^\frac{\alpha_0}{n-d}\geq M_0|z|^{\alpha_0}=M_0|z|^{\alpha_0-\alpha}|z|^\alpha\geq M_0 R^{\alpha_0-\alpha}|z|^\alpha=M|z|^\alpha
	$$
for all $z\in\mathbb{R}^{n-d}_+\cap B^{n-d}_R$.	Therefore, the restriction of $f$ to $\Gamma\cap B_R\subset B^d_R\times \big(\mathbb{R}^{n-d}_{\geq0}\cap B^{n-d}_R\big)$ gives the required function $v$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $v$ be the function given by Lemma \ref{lemma_barrier3}, where we take the same $M$ as in \eqref{eqn_proofexistence0.1} and take $R$ large enough such that $\Omega\subset\Gamma\cap B_R$. Using the classical existence result (Lemma \ref{lemma_existence}), we obtain a sequence $(u_k)_{k=1,2,\cdots}$ of convex solutions to equation \eqref{eqn_proofexistence0} with truncated right-hand sides:
$$
\det\mathsf{D}^2u_k=\min\{g, k\}\ \text{ in }\Omega,\quad u_k|_{\partial\Omega}=0.
$$
By \eqref{eqn_proofexistence0.1} and \eqref{eqn_proofexistence0.2}, we have
$$
\det\mathsf{D}^2u_k\leq \det\mathsf{D}^2u_{k+1}\leq \det\mathsf{D}^2v\ \ \text{ in }\Omega,
$$
whereas $u_k|_{\partial\Omega}=u_{k+1}|_{\partial\Omega}=0\geq v|_{\partial\Omega}$, so the comparison principle (Lemma \ref{lemma_comparison}) gives
$$
u_k\geq u_{k+1}\geq v \ \text{ in }\Omega.
$$
Therefore, the pointwise limit function
$$
u:\Omega\to\mathbb{R},\quad u(x):=\lim_{k\to\infty}u_k(x)
$$
is well defined. By Lemma \ref{lemma_uniform}, $u$ is also convex and the convergence $u_k\to u$ is uniform on compact subsets of $\Omega$. Then it follows from the stability of Monge-Amp\`ere measures (Lemma \ref{lemma_stability}) that 
$$
\det\mathsf{D}^2u=\lim_{k\to\infty}\det\mathsf{D}^2u_k=g.
$$ 

To show that $u$ provides a solution to \eqref{eqn_proofexistence0}, it only remains to check that
\begin{equation}\label{eqn_proofexistence1}
\liminf_{x\in\Omega,\ x\to x_0}u(x)=0
\end{equation}
for all $x_0\in\partial\Omega$, which is a necessary and sufficient condition for $u$ to be extendable to a continuous convex function on $\overline{\Omega}$ with $u|_{\partial\Omega}=0$ (see Remark \ref{rk_extension}). For $x_0\in F=\partial\Omega\cap L$, \eqref{eqn_proofexistence1} holds because
$$
0\geq \liminf_{x\in\Omega,\ x\to x_0}u(x)\geq \liminf_{x\in\Omega,\ x\to x_0}v(x)=v(x_0)=0.
$$
At $x_0\in \partial\Omega\setminus L$, although $v$ might not vanish, we can still deduce \eqref{eqn_proofexistence1} from the Alexandrov maximum principle. We now present a unified proof of \eqref{eqn_proofexistence1} for all $x_0\in\partial\Omega$.

Given $\epsilon>0$, consider the level sets
$$
E_{k,\epsilon}:=\big\{x\in\Omega\,\big|\,u_k\leq-\epsilon\big\},\quad E_\epsilon:=\big\{x\in\Omega\,\big|\,v\leq-\epsilon\big\}.
$$
Note that $u_k\geq v$ implies $E_{k,\epsilon}\subset E_\epsilon$.
The key to the proof is the fact that the mass of $E_{k,\epsilon}$ under the Monge-Amp\`ere measure of $u_k$ has an upper bound independent of $k$:
\begin{equation}\label{eqn_proofexistence2}
\mathcal{M}u_k(E_{k,\epsilon})\leq \mathcal{M}u_k(E_{\epsilon})\leq\mathcal{M}v(E_\epsilon)<+\infty,
\end{equation}
where the first ``$\leq$'' follows from $E_{k,\epsilon}\subset E_\epsilon$, the second from $\det\mathsf{D}^2 u_k\leq \det \mathsf{D}^2v$, and the last ``$<$'' holds  because $E_\epsilon$ is bounded away from the singular locus $L$ of $\det\mathsf{D}^2v$.

Since $u_k|_{\partial\Omega}=0$, $E_{k,\epsilon}$ is a compact convex set and we have $u_k|_{\partial E_{k,\epsilon}}=-\epsilon$. Therefore, we can apply the Alexandrov maximum principle (Lemma \ref{lemma_AlexandrovMP}) to the function $u_k+\epsilon$ on $E_{k,\epsilon}$. In view of \eqref{eqn_proofexistence2}, this gives
$$
u_k(x)\geq-\epsilon-C\, {\mathrm{dist}}(x,\partial E_{k,\epsilon})^\frac{1}{n}\ \ \text{ for all }x\in E_{k,\epsilon},
$$
where the constant $C=C(n,{\mathrm{diam}}(\Omega),\mathcal{M}v(E_\epsilon))>0$  depends on $\epsilon$ but not on $k$. Since ${\mathrm{dist}}(x,\partial E_{k,\epsilon})< {\mathrm{dist}}(x,\partial\Omega)$ for $x\in E_{k,\epsilon}$ and $u_k(x)>-\epsilon$ for $x\in \Omega\setminus E_{k,\epsilon}$, it follows that
$$
u_k(x)\geq -\epsilon-C\,{\mathrm{dist}}(x,\partial\Omega)^\frac{1}{n}\ \ \text{ for all }x\in\Omega.
$$
The same holds for $u(x)$ by letting $k\to\infty$. Therefore, for any $x_0\in\partial\Omega$, we have
$$
0\geq \liminf_{x\in\Omega,\,x\to x_0}u(x)\geq -\epsilon -C\liminf_{x\in\Omega,\,x\to x_0}{\mathrm{dist}}(x,\partial\Omega)^\frac{1}{n}=-\epsilon.
$$
Since $\epsilon>0$ is arbitrary, this implies \eqref{eqn_proofexistence1} and completes the proof.
